title: Start the two-user API case study
command:
cd "$HOME/kali-lab/advanced-casebook"
python3 lab_app.py --mode vulnerable --port 8901
explanation: Copy examples/advanced-casebook into the shown Kali folder first. Keep this server in Terminal A.
options: The listener is fixed to 127.0.0.1. Alice/alice-lab and Bob/bob-lab are public training accounts; 123456 is a fake MFA code. Restart resets state. This is not production authentication.
result: A disposable vulnerable fixture; use Terminal B for the next lesson.

title: Compare vulnerable and fixed authorization
command:
python3 exercise.py --expect vulnerable --case api
# After stopping and restarting Terminal A with --mode fixed:
python3 exercise.py --expect fixed --case api
explanation: The client logs in synthetic users and checks object, property, legacy-route and limit behavior.
options: Run the second command only after changing the server mode. passed means observed results match that mode; vulnerable-mode pass deliberately confirms the weakness.
result: Eight API checks pass against each corresponding mode; the same fixed expectations fail against vulnerable behavior.

title: Extend coverage to schemas, GraphQL and webhooks
command:
python3 exercise.py --expect fixed --case webhook
python3 -m unittest -v test_lab.LabTests.test_stale_webhook
explanation: The webhook fixture signs raw bytes with a public training HMAC key, checks timestamp freshness and rejects repeated event IDs.
options: For a real GraphQL service, create field/resolver permission tests using two identities and bound depth, aliases, pagination and complexity. For REST, validate request/response schemas and inventory old API versions. The supplied app has no GraphQL engine.
result: A valid signed event is accepted; bad signature, stale proof and replay fail. Schema validation and authorization remain separate checks.

title: Exercise the session state transitions
command:
python3 exercise.py --expect vulnerable --case auth
# Restart the app in fixed mode before this command:
python3 exercise.py --expect fixed --case auth
explanation: Compare four session-lifecycle expectations in the two teaching modes.
options: The client checks the pending boundary, token rotation, old-token handling and logout. Use test_lab for expiry and incorrect-MFA cases. Capture only redacted evidence.
result: Fixed mode rejects incomplete/old sessions while a correctly completed session remains usable.

title: Understand transaction correlation before federation
command: python3 auth_binding.py
explanation: Run a pure data model that compares one expected login transaction against a response.
options: Expect one true match and false after each changed field. In a real OIDC integration, perform these context checks in addition to cryptographic token verification and provider-specific protocol requirements.
result: A clear demonstration that a signed-looking claim set still needs the correct transaction and audience.

title: Review recovery and account linking
command:
Write the required proof for password reset, MFA reset and account linking.
Bind each proof to one user, action and expiry.
Check single use and reauthentication requirements.
Ensure failed recovery leaves existing account ownership unchanged.
explanation: Recovery and linking are alternative paths to account control and deserve their own state diagrams.
options: Use two synthetic accounts and a lab inbox in a separately configured identity app. Do not infer security from identical success/error messages alone; inspect state changes, tokens and audit events.
result: A test matrix for valid, expired, reused, wrong-user and wrong-action proofs.

title: Reproduce a race deterministically
command: python3 race_demo.py
explanation: A barrier coordinates the two synthetic workers so the vulnerable case is repeatable.
options: The vulnerable branch reads before the barrier and writes afterward; the fixed branch performs decision/update under one lock. No external traffic or real transaction is involved.
result: vulnerable successes: 2; fixed successes: 1.

title: Verify the actual HTTP invariant
command:
python3 -m unittest -v test_lab.LabTests.test_atomic_http_redemption
# With a freshly restarted fixed server:
python3 exercise.py --case logic --expect fixed
explanation: Test the implemented coupon route with concurrent requests and a sequential duplicate.
options: The unittest owns a fresh temporary server. The separate exercise uses your running server and consumes its coupon; restart before repeating.
result: Exactly one concurrent request succeeds; later duplicate redemption returns 409.

title: Design idempotency and payment-state rules
command:
Operation | Idempotency scope | Allowed transition | Durable evidence
Create order | User + request key | Draft -> Pending | Unique order ID
Confirm payment | Verified provider event | Pending -> Paid | Deduplicated event ID
Refund | Authorized refund key | Paid -> Refunded | Transaction record
explanation: Document business invariants before adding parallel tests.
options: Bind idempotency keys to the authenticated caller and operation; reject key reuse with a different request. Validate provider callbacks independently. Retries must not create extra financial side effects.
result: A worksheet for a separate payment sandbox; the lab coupon does not implement a payment processor.

title: Trace the API code without executing arbitrary input
command:
nl -ba lab_app.py | less
nl -ba browser.js | less
explanation: Read the handlers and follow data from request to result.
options: Identify body size/schema checks, session stage, owner/tenant test, field allowlist and audit record. In browser.js locate origin, source, schema and textContent. Press q to leave less.
result: A source-to-behavior map for the lab findings.

title: Compare Django object lookup boundaries
command:
# Review sketch, not a standalone program.
# Weak boundary: authenticated user may still request another owner object.
invoice = get_object_or_404(Invoice, pk=invoice_id)

# Scoped lookup: tenant context must come from validated server-side identity.
invoice = get_object_or_404(
    Invoice, pk=invoice_id, owner=request.user, tenant_id=request.tenant.id
)
explanation: An authenticated route still needs object-level authorization.
options: This assumes get_object_or_404 is imported, Invoice exists, login is enforced and request.tenant is trusted middleware context. For shared access or administrators, encode the real policy rather than blindly applying this owner-only sketch.
result: A review pattern showing where authorization belongs; test with actual project fixtures before use.

title: Compare JavaScript rendering and validation
explanation: Validate data shape and choose an API that preserves text semantics.
options: The caller must independently validate message origin/source. Length checking does not sanitize HTML; textContent avoids parsing the string as markup in this sink.
result: Both the trust decision and rendering operation are reviewed.

title: Inspect the browser fixture and CSP
command:
Open http://127.0.0.1:8901/ in your lab browser.
Open Developer Tools > Network, reload and select the document.
Inspect Content-Security-Policy and browser.js.
Confirm the initial <b> text appears literally.
explanation: Use the fixed local app. No external assets are requested by the page.
options: The policy allows same-origin scripts and blocks framing through frame-ancestors. Inspect actual browser behavior rather than treating a header presence check as sufficient evidence.
result: A browser observation with policy and DOM context.

title: Exercise the message contract
explanation: Run only in the console of the local training page.
options: This self-message uses a known source for the standalone exercise. A real parent/iframe integration should bind expectedSource to its intended frame, not accept all windows sharing an origin.
result: Only the valid message updates output text.

title: Test browser policy logic independently
command: node browser_tests.cjs
explanation: Check valid message, wrong origin, wrong source, oversized payload and null payload.
options: The tests import the pure validator without a DOM. Keep separate browser checks for script loading, CSP and actual window identities.
result: Five passing policy cases; no claim that a browser was automatically tested.

title: Build the data-flow inventory
command:
Asset | Actor | Entry point | Trust boundary | Required control
Invoice | Alice/Bob | GET /api/invoices/id | User -> API | Owner + tenant
Session | Login client | POST /mfa | Pending -> Complete | Proof + rotation
Coupon | Signed-in user | POST /redeem | Request -> Shared state | Atomic single use
Event | Provider fixture | POST /webhook | External -> API | Signature + freshness + replay check
explanation: Use threat_model.md to extend this table with data stores and outbound dependencies.
options: State assumptions explicitly. The lab stores data in memory; a production database, proxy and identity provider introduce additional boundaries.
result: An application-specific threat model rather than a generic list of tool names.

title: Connect threats to tests
command:
Threat | Existing verification | Coverage gap
Cross-user invoice read | test_fixed_end_to_end | Shared-role policies absent
Pending session access | auth exercise | Real identity provider absent
Concurrent redemption | test_atomic_http_redemption | Multi-process database absent
Forged/replayed event | webhook exercise | Provider key rotation absent
explanation: Test names are evidence of coverage only when their setup, assertions and failure behavior are understood.
options: Run the named tests, inspect what they actually assert and add a separate planned test for each missing production component.
result: A traceable list of verified requirements and open questions.

title: Prioritize and maintain the model
command:
For each threat record: affected asset, preconditions, likely impact and confidence.
Assign mitigation owner and verification step.
Record accepted assumptions and expiry/review date.
Update the model when a route, dependency or trust relationship changes.
explanation: Threat modeling is a repeatable design activity, not a one-time score.
options: Use the supplied synthetic scenario to practise decisions. Keep risk severity distinct from how certain the evidence is; do not fabricate a precise score without its assumptions.
result: A living review checklist with actionable owners.

title: Run the complete regression suite
command:
python3 -m unittest -v test_lab
node browser_tests.cjs
explanation: The Python suite starts and stops its own servers on ephemeral loopback ports.
options: There are 12 Python test methods and five Node assertions. Do not depend on a manually running fixture or previous coupon state. Read failures before rerunning.
result: All tests pass, including the test that proves fixed expectations detect the vulnerable implementation.

title: Prove the tests notice the missing control
command: python3 -m unittest -v test_lab.LabTests.test_fixed_expectations_detect_vulnerable
explanation: This meta-test enables vulnerable behavior and asserts that the fixed API checks do not all pass.
options: Without an effective negative test, a passing suite can hide missing coverage. Inspect the returned failed checks in exercise.run when debugging, while keeping tokens out of reports.
result: A passing meta-test that confirms the detector observes the intended weakness.

title: Prepare a local CI-style check
command:
python3 -m compileall -q lab_app.py exercise.py race_demo.py auth_binding.py
python3 -m unittest -v test_lab
node --check browser.js
node browser_tests.cjs
explanation: Run syntax checks plus behavioral tests as separate stages.
options: Configure your CI runner to stop on nonzero exit instead of blindly executing a shell list and returning only the final command status. Pin a supported runtime and avoid real credentials or internet dependencies in these fixtures.
result: A repeatable verification sequence suitable for adapting to your own pipeline.

title: Collect the vulnerable-mode baseline
command: python3 exercise.py --expect vulnerable --case all > vulnerable-observations.json
explanation: Run against a freshly restarted vulnerable fixture.
options: The report contains check names and booleans, not tokens or invoice bodies. It is a mode comparison; add manual policy and impact explanation in report_template.md.
result: A saved synthetic baseline, replacing the named report if it exists.

title: Retest the fixed implementation
command:
python3 exercise.py --expect fixed --case all > fixed-observations.json
python3 -m unittest -v test_lab
explanation: First stop and restart the manual fixture in fixed mode.
options: The full exercise consumes coupon state, so restart before repeating. Compare the meaning of the checks in both reports; both overall passed values mean matched expectations, not equal security.
result: Fixed controls meet the tested requirements while normal owner and display-name operations remain usable.

title: Write and review the assessment report
command:
Scope and synthetic target
Authentication and roles used
Finding: expected policy versus observed behavior
Minimal redacted reproduction
Root cause and affected code path
Impact with assumptions
Fix and positive/negative retest evidence
Coverage gaps and follow-up work
explanation: Use report_template.md and compare your explanation with sample_finding.md.
options: Keep risk severity tied to actual impact and scope. Do not claim all API features were assessed: GraphQL, real federation, payments and production deployment are explicitly outside this fixture.
result: A reproducible training report with honest limits.
